description: We are building a a flutter backed, simulation-driven resource management dashboard designed to train the next generation of space explorers. By combining clean architecture with interactive UI design, we are turning complex aerospace logic into an intuitive, gamified learning experience.
summary:
LunarQuest is a free browser game that makes kids aged 7–12 the Mission Commander of a four-person crew on a lunar outpost. Over 14 days, players must protect three resources: Life Support, Power and Radiation. Along the way they face seven real situations, from moon dust on the solar panels to a solar storm. Every situation offers two choices, and neither one is free. Running the science lab costs power. Finishing your samples during a storm costs radiation. After each decision, a Real Space Fact explains the science and names its NASA source.

LunarQuest answers the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by teaching how astronauts think, not just what they know: weigh trade-offs, plan ahead and live with the consequences. The numbers are real. They include 0.85 kg of oxygen per astronaut per day from the ISS and NASA's 250 mSv solar-storm radiation limit. The Day 7 storm replays one of seven archived solar flares from NASA's DONKI database, so every run is different.

This matters because most kids only watch space. LunarQuest lets them make the decisions. It runs on any phone, tablet or laptop, with no download and no account.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

LunarQuest is a decision-making game that trains kids aged 7–12 to think like astronauts. The player commands a four-person crew at a lunar outpost near the Moon's South Pole for 14 Earth days. Their job is to keep the crew alive while doing as much science as possible.

HOW IT WORKS

Each day follows four steps:

1. Observe: a short story card describes what is happening at the outpost.

2. Investigate: the player taps equipment on an interactive outpost map to find the problem.

3. Decide: the player picks one of two options. Each option gains something and gives something up.

4. Learn: a Real Space Fact explains the science behind the choice and names its NASA source.

Three resources are tracked the whole time, each based on a real rule:

- Life Support: each astronaut breathes 0.85 kg of oxygen per day (NASA ISS data).

- Power: solar panels charge the battery, and moon dust cuts their output in half.

- Radiation: the dose adds up and never goes away. Reaching 250 mSv (NASA's solar-storm limit) ends the mission.

Choices carry forward. Skip cleaning the panels on Day 3 and the power drains every day after. If any resource runs out, the mission is aborted and the game explains why. If the crew survives, the player earns up to 5 Science Stars.

BENEFITS

- Teaches real thinking skills: weighing trade-offs, planning ahead and accepting consequences, which is how real mission control works.

- Teaches real science: oxygen use, solar power, moon dust, radiation and space weather, all in plain words.

- Builds trust in sources: every fact names where it came from, which shows kids that science is something you can check.

- Reaches everyone: it is free and runs in any web browser on a phone, tablet or laptop, with no download, account or personal data.

INTENDED IMPACT

Most kids only watch space. LunarQuest lets them make the decisions. We want a child to finish a mission understanding why astronauts shelter during a solar storm, why oxygen is precious, and why every choice in space has a price. We also want them to replay the game to try a different strategy. Teachers can use one mission as a 15-minute classroom activity to start a discussion.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Languages: TypeScript, HTML and CSS

- Framework: React with Vite

- Styling and animation: Tailwind CSS and Motion

- Game state: Zustand

- Data validation: Zod (every mission is a JSON file checked against a schema)

- Testing: Vitest, with 43 automated tests covering the game engine, scoring, map logic and mission data

- Hosting: Vercel (static site, first load of about 135 kB)

- NASA data: the DONKI space weather database, NASA-STD-3001, ISS life support reports, NASA technical reports (NTRS) and NASA mission pages (15 sources in total)

The game rules live in a pure TypeScript engine, separate from the user interface, so they can be tested on their own. The mission content lives in data files, so new missions can be added without changing the code.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

- No quiz questions: there are no right or wrong answers, only trade-offs. Even a "safe" choice costs something.

- Real space weather: the Day 7 solar storm replays one of seven real flares from NASA's archive, for example the X8.2 flare of 10 September 2017. Some carry fast particles that pass through spacesuits, so the same choice can be safe in one game and dangerous in the next.

- Feels like a movie: on a phone held sideways, the outpost map fills the screen and each day unfolds step by step.

- A robot guide: a friendly robot reacts to every choice and keeps the tone encouraging, even when a mission fails.

FACTORS OUR TEAM CONSIDERED

- Age: plain words, one idea per screen, large buttons and short text for readers aged 7–12.

- Accuracy: every science fact was checked against a NASA page that we opened and read. Where a number is a game design choice (for example battery size), we say so openly in our documentation.

- Fairness: we simulated all 128 possible choice paths against every storm type. A balanced player always survives, so the game is challenging but never unfair.

- Access: it works on cheap phones and slow connections, needs no account and collects no personal data.

- Accessibility: keyboard controls, screen-reader labels and support for reduced motion.

- Honesty: archived solar storms are clearly labelled as archived NASA data, never as live.
